So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you for having heard me.
I knew you hear me at all times; yet I spoke on account of the crowd that stands here, that they may come to believe you sent me.”
With these words he cried out with a great voice, “Lazarus, here, outside!”
The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth, and his face wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus says to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”
So, many of the Jews who had come to visit Mary, and who had watched what he did, put their faith in him.
But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
The chief priests and the Pharisees therefore convened the council{i} and said, “What are we doing? Here is this man working many signs.
If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place{j} and our nation.”
But one of them, Caiaphas,{k} who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,
nor do you consider that it is to your advantage for one man to die on behalf of the people, rather than for the entire nation to be lost.”
It was not from himself that he said this; rather, as high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die on behalf of the nation,
and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.
From that day, then, their counsel was to put him to death.
For this reason Jesus no longer walked about in public among the Jews. He left that place for the country close to the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim,{l} and stayed there with the disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up from the countryside to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.
They were looking for Jesus, and as they stood in the temple they said to one another, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they might arrest him.

notes.text: Lazarus: a Greek form of Hebrew *Eleazar*, “God has helped.”
Mary: Greek *Mariam* or *Maria*, from Hebrew *Miryam* (Miriam), a name of uncertain meaning.
Martha: Aramaic, “lady” or “mistress.”
The anointing is narrated in 12:1–8; John refers to it here as already known to his readers.
Thomas … the Twin: *Thomas* is from Aramaic *toma*, “twin,” and Greek *Didymos* also means “twin.”
Less than two miles: literally “about fifteen stadia,” about 1¾ miles (2.8 km).
I am the resurrection and the life: the fifth “I am” saying with a predicate (see the note on 6:20). P45 and a few other witnesses are reported to omit “and the life.”

Deeply moved in spirit: Greek *enebrimēsato*, a strong word that elsewhere expresses indignation or stern rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5); here perhaps anger at the power of death, or intense distress. So also in 11:38.
Council: Greek *synedrion*, the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest.
Our place: probably the temple (compare Acts 6:13–14), or perhaps Jerusalem or the council’s position.
Caiaphas: Joseph Caiaphas, high priest AD 18–36, son-in-law of Annas (18:13). *That year* means “in that fateful year.”
Ephraim: perhaps et-Taiyibeh, about 12 miles (19 km) northeast of Jerusalem. The name means “doubly fruitful” (Gen 41:52).

verses.text: Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.
There they gave a dinner for him. Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with him.
Then Mary took a pound{a} of very costly perfume, pure nard,{b} anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who was about to betray him, says,
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred days’ wages,{c} and the proceeds given to the poor?”
He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; he kept the money bag and used to help himself to what was put in it.
So Jesus said, “Let her alone; she was to keep it for the day of my burial.{d}
For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.”
Then a large crowd of the Jews found out he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake alone, but to see Lazarus too, whom he had raised from the dead.
The chief priests, however, resolved to kill Lazarus also,
because many of the Jews were leaving them for his sake and putting their faith in Jesus.
On the following day the large crowd who had come up for the feast, hearing that Jesus was on his way into Jerusalem,
So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!{e} Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,{f} even the King of Israel!”
Jesus came upon a young donkey and seated himself on it, just as Scripture says,
“Fear not, daughter of Zion; look, your king comes, sitting on the colt of a donkey.”{g}
His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus was glorified, they remembered that these things had been written about him and that they had done these things to him.
The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead kept bearing witness.
That was the reason the crowd went to meet him: they had heard that he had performed this sign.
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see, you are getting nowhere. Look, the world has gone after him!”
Among those who went up to worship at the festival were some Greeks.
They approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and made a request of him: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”
Philip goes and tells Andrew; Andrew and Philip go and tell Jesus.
And Jesus answers them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
Amen, amen, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
The one who loves his life is losing it, and the one who hates his life in this world will guard it to life eternal.
If anyone would serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be too. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.
“Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’? But it was for this very reason that I came to this hour.
Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came out of heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
The crowd standing there heard it and said it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus replied, “It was not on my account that this voice came, but on yours.
Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”{h}
He said this to indicate by what kind of death he was going to die.
The crowd answered him, “We have heard out of the Law that the Messiah abides forever.{i} So how do you say the Son of Man has to be lifted up? Who is he, this Son of Man?”

Jesus then said to them, “For only a short time more the light is with you. Keep walking as long as you have the light, lest darkness seize you; the one who walks in darkness has no idea where he goes.
While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become children of light.” After Jesus had said this, he went away and hid himself from them.
But for all the signs he had done in their sight, they did not believe in him,
so that the word spoken by Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what we have heard? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”{j}
That is why they could not believe; for again Isaiah said,
“He has made their eyes blind and their heart hard, lest they see with the eyes and grasp with the heart and turn back, and I heal them.”{k}
Isaiah said these things because{l} he saw his glory and spoke about him.
Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so as not to be put out of the synagogue;
They loved the glory people give more than the glory God gives.
Then Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me.
And whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.
I, a light, have come into the world, that whoever believes in me may not be left in the dark.
If someone hears my sayings and fails to keep them, it is not I who judge him. I came not to condemn the world but to save it.
Whoever sets me aside and will not accept my sayings has one who judges him: the very word I have spoken will be his judge on the last day.
I did not speak from myself; the Father who sent me gave me his own command about what I should say and how I should speak.
And I know that his command is life eternal. So the things I speak, I speak as the Father has said them to me.”

notes.text: A pound: literally “a litra,” the Roman pound (Latin *libra*), about 12 ounces (327 g).
Pure nard: Greek *nardos pistikē*, an aromatic oil made from a plant of the Himalayas; the meaning of *pistikē* is uncertain (perhaps “genuine” or a place name).
Three hundred days’ wages: literally “three hundred denarii,” about a year’s wages for a laborer. See the note on 6:7.

She was to keep it for the day of my burial: the Greek is difficult. Many later manuscripts read “she has kept it for the day of my burial.” Others take it as “Let her keep it for the day of my burial.”
Hosanna: a Greek transliteration of Hebrew *hoshiah na*, “Save, we pray!” (Ps 118:25), which had become a shout of praise.
Ps 118:26. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Zech 9:9, abbreviated; *do not be afraid* may come from Isa 40:9 or Zeph 3:16. *Zion* is the hill of Jerusalem, and by extension the city and its people.
All people: P66 (as reported), Sinaiticus (first hand), Codex Bezae and the Latin versions read “all things.”
Compare Ps 89:36–37; Isa 9:7; Ezek 37:25; Dan 7:14. *The Law* here means the Scriptures generally.
Isa 53:1, following the Greek Old Testament, which adds the opening “Lord” (addressed to God). In the Hebrew text, “the arm of the Lord” is “the arm of Yahweh.”
Isa 6:10, in a form that differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament.
Because: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts; many later manuscripts read “when.” Isaiah’s vision of the Lord’s glory is in Isa 6:1–5.
